events.title: Spanish conquest and colony
hints: Columbus landed in 1493, and a former companion governed the island from 1508.
The Taíno were put to work in gold washing, and a major revolt in 1511 was crushed.
Sugar and then coffee estates relied on enslaved Africans until abolition in 1873, and Spain lost the island in 1898.
events.summary: Spain claimed the island in 1493, and Juan Ponce de León led the colonisation from 1508. Taíno labour in gold washing and disease reduced the Indigenous population, and enslaved Africans were brought for sugar and later coffee. Slavery was abolished in 1873 and Spain ceded the island in 1898.

events.title: US annexation and the Foraker Act
hints: After a 1898 war the island was ceded by a European power and occupied by American forces.
The 1900 Foraker Act set up a government whose governor and upper house were appointed from outside.
The status of a commonwealth was adopted in 1952.
events.summary: Spain ceded the island under the 1898 Treaty of Paris. The 1900 Foraker Act created a civil government with an appointed governor and upper house, and US corporations took over much of the sugar economy. Residents gained US citizenship in 1917 and a commonwealth constitution in 1952.

events.title: US Navy use of Vieques
hints: In 1941 the navy expropriated about two thirds of a small island east of the main island.
The land was used for decades for live-fire bombing and amphibious training.
A civilian death in 1999 sparked mass protests, and the bombing ended in 2003.
events.summary: Starting in 1941 the US Navy took over most of Vieques and used it for naval gunfire, bombing and training exercises. Residents were displaced, and the accidental death of a civilian guard in 1999 led to mass protests. Live-fire training ended in 2003.
